Convert GTFS to GPS-like data given a spatial resolution

Source: R/gtfs2gps.R
gtfs2gps.Rd

Convert GTFS data to GPS format by sampling points using a given spatial resolution. This function creates additional points in order to guarantee that two points in a same trip will have at most a given distance, indicated as a spatial resolution.

Stops without times are placed along the shape at constant speed between the timed stops. fix_gtfs can clean a feed before converting it (e.g. duplicated rows and unused ids), but the stop times it interpolates may give spiky or infinite speeds here.

Usage

gtfs2gps(
  gtfs_data,
  spatial_resolution = 100,
  parallel = NULL,
  ncores = 2,
  strategy = NULL,
  filepath = NULL,
  compress = FALSE,
  snap_method = NULL,
  continue = FALSE,
  quiet = FALSE
)

Arguments

gtfs_data

A path to a GTFS file to be converted to GPS, or a GTFS data represented as a list of data.tables.

spatial_resolution

The spatial resolution in meters: a number of at least 1, or a units length. Default is 100m. This function only creates points in order to guarantee that consecutive points are at most spatial_resolution metres apart. If a given shape has two consecutive points with a distance lower than the spatial resolution, the algorithm will not remove such points.

parallel

This argument is deprecated and ignored. Please use argument ncores instead.

ncores

Number of threads used. Defaults to 2. If Inf, it uses all threads available, as given by data.table::getDTthreads().

strategy

This argument is deprecated and ignored. Please use argument ncores instead.

filepath

Output file path. As default, the output is returned when gtfs2gps finishes. When this argument is set, each shape is saved into a txt file within filepath, named after its shape_id. Characters that can't be in a file name on some systems (such as /, : or *) and % are written as %XX, their hexadecimal code, so utils::URLdecode() gives the id back (e.g. "a/b" is saved as a%2Fb.txt). In this case, no output is returned. See argument compress for another option.

compress

Argument that can be used only with filepath. When TRUE, it compresses the output files by saving them using .rds format. Default value is FALSE. Note that compress guarantees that the data saved will be read in the same way as it was created in R. If not compress, the txt extension requires the data to be converted from ITime to string, and therefore they need to be manually converted back to ITime to be properly handled by gtfs2gps.

snap_method

This argument is deprecated and ignored. Stops are now located along the shapes with gtfstools::interpolate_shape_dist_traveled() (see details).

continue

Argument that can be used only with filepath. When TRUE, it skips processing the shape identifiers that were already saved into files. It is useful to continue processing a GTFS file that was stopped for some reason. Default value is FALSE.

quiet

Hide messages while processing the data. Defaults to FALSE.

Value

A data.table, where each row represents a GPS point. The following columns are returned (units of measurement in parenthesis): dist and cumdist (meters), cumtime (seconds), shape_pt_lon and shape_pt_lat (degrees), speed (km/h), timestamp (data.table::ITime, wrapped at midnight). Speed, dist, cumdist and cumtime are rounded to 3 decimal places (also when written to filepath), except speeds closer to zero than that, which keep their value (such as the 1e-12 km/h of stops). With filepath, each shape is written to a file and NULL is returned.

Details

Before converting, the feed is cleaned with gtfstools::remove_duplicates() and gtfstools::remove_unused_ids(), and trips with an NA trip_id are dropped. Errors and warnings raised by the package have classes starting with gtfs2gps_ (e.g. gtfs2gps_nothing_converted_error), and deprecation warnings with deprecated_, so they can be caught.

After creating geometry points for a given shape id, the gtfs2gps() function snaps the stops to the route geometry. The stops of each trip are located along the shape with gtfstools::interpolate_shape_dist_traveled(), which projects each stop onto the shape keeping the stops in their stop_sequence order, so that loops and shapes that pass by the same place more than once are handled. Each stop is then snapped to the nearest point of the shape in high resolution, moved forward when needed so that each stop has a point of its own. Distances are great-circle distances on the sphere used by the s2 and sf packages, with a radius of 6,371,010 m.

Each trip runs from its first to its last stop with a departure time: shape points (and stops without times) before the first one and after the last one have no time to be interpolated from, and are not returned. The speed, cumdist, and cumtime are based on the difference of distance and time between the current and previous row of the same trip. It means that the first data point of each trip, at its first stop, represents a stationary vehicle, with dist, cumdist and cumtime equal to zero: cumdist is the distance travelled from the first stop. Unrealistic speeds are best fixed in the GTFS before converting it, with gtfstools::set_max_speed() and gtfstools::set_min_speed(). Two stops at the same place and time give an NA speed.

Each stop is presented as two data points for each trip in the output. The timestamp value in the first data point represents the time when the vehicle arrived at that stop (corresponding the arrival_time column in the stop_times.txt file), while the timestamp in the second data point represents the time when the vehicle departed from that stop (corresponding the departure_time column in the stop_times.txt file). The second point considers that the vehicle is stationary at the stop, immediately before departing.

Some GTFS feeds do not report embark/disembark times (so arrival_time and departure_time are identical at the same stop). In this case, gtfstools::set_dwell_time() or gtfstools::set_min_dwell_time() can set the time vehicles spend at stops to embark/disembark passengers.

To avoid division by zero, the minimum speed of vehicles in the output is 1e-12 km/h, so that vehicles are never completely stopped.

Examples

library(gtfs2gps)

gtfs <- read_gtfs(system.file("extdata/poa.zip", package = "gtfs2gps")) |>
  gtfstools::filter_by_shape_id("T2-1") |>
  filter_single_trip()
#> Unzipped the following files to /tmp/RtmphjGwSa/gtfsio:
#>   * agency.txt
#>   * calendar.txt
#>   * routes.txt
#>   * shapes.txt
#>   * stop_times.txt
#>   * stops.txt
#>   * trips.txt
#> Reading agency
#> Reading calendar
#> Reading routes
#> Reading shapes
#> Reading stop_times
#> Reading stops
#> Reading trips

poa_gps <- gtfs2gps(gtfs, quiet = TRUE)
